metadata.file_name: Euro J of Education - 2025 - Koca Guler - Data Mining on the Fundamental Factors Influencing Mathematics Achievement .pdf
metadata.title: Data Mining on the Fundamental Factors Influencing Mathematics Achievement: Traditional and Modern Perspectives

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 mathematics achievement for three national samples (England, Turkey, South Africa) and models the nested structure of students within schools and schools within countries. The authors report using plausible values by taking the mean of five plausible values as the dependent variable, but they do not report any application of TIMSS sampling weights or replicate weights in the analysis. Because the paper focuses on linear mixed models (LMM) and ML methods designed for hierarchical data (REEM-tree and GP boosting), it is unclear whether complex survey weighting was incorporated; the manuscript does not name any TIMSS weight variables (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures. Analysts using the TIMSS International Database should consider applying the official TIMSS sampling weights and appropriate variance estimation when estimating uncertainty, especially given the clustered sampling design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that the original TIMSS dataset contains a significant amount of missing data and that some teacher/home datasets are excluded for England due to excessive missingness, but it does not specify a formal missing-data handling method (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation, or a defined imputation rule) for the analytic variables. Although REEM-tree is described as being able to handle missing values in attributes during tree construction, the manuscript does not document how missingness was treated consistently across all three approaches (LMM, REEM-tree, GP boosting). This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data handling at the level of the final analytic dataset.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 mathematics data from three countries selected for contrast in achievement and development level: England, Turkey, and South Africa. The dependent variable is constructed as the mean of the five TIMSS plausible values for mathematics achievement (rather than using PVs individually). The analysis is restricted to student-level predictors that are available with acceptable missingness; teacher data are excluded due to excessive missing values in England, and home data are entirely unavailable for England. Because TIMSS class-level information is not distinguishable between school and class effects in Turkey and South Africa (and England has one class per school except for 20 schools), the models are built with a two-level structure: schools nested within countries (random effects), rather than including a class level.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics (England, Turkey, South Africa; PV mean outcome)
main_findings.performance_metrics: LMM: RMSE 61.069, MAE 48.761, MAPE 11.680. REEM-tree: RMSE 61.032, MAE 48.611, MAPE 11.611. GP boosting: RMSE 59.923, MAE 47.797, MAPE 11.415. (Best = lowest error metrics: GP boosting.)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics the study leveraged Mathematical tendency factor, Emotional factor (math), SES, Number of books at home, and Born in the country to predict mathematics achievement (mean of five plausible values), finding that Mathematical tendency and Emotional factors were the most consistently important positive predictors across LMM, REEM-tree, and GP boosting, while gender showed negligible impact. The best predictive performance was achieved by GP boosting with lower RMSE/MAE/MAPE than LMM and REEM-tree, indicating that strengthening students’ math-related motivation and reducing math anxiety may improve achievement while ML methods that respect hierarchical structure can provide more accurate prediction than standard mixed models, though causality cannot be inferred from these cross-sectional associations. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 mathematics achievement for three national samples (England, Turkey, South Africa; N=2521, 3334, 7747) using a two-level hierarchical setup with schools nested within countries. Because TIMSS provides five plausible values, the authors construct the dependent variable as the mean of the five PVs. They compare a classical linear mixed model (LMM) with two ML approaches designed for nested data: REEM-tree and GP boosting, using an 80/20 random train-test split and reporting RMSE, MAE, and MAPE. GP boosting performs best (RMSE=59.923, MAE=47.797, MAPE=11.415), followed closely by REEM-tree, while LMM yields slightly higher errors (RMSE=61.069, MAE=48.761, MAPE=11.680). Across methods, mathematical tendency and emotional factors are the strongest predictors, whereas gender has negligible predictive/inferential contribution. Limitations include unclear survey-weight usage and incomplete documentation of missing-data handling, even though the paper notes substantial missingness and variable exclusions.
